newsitem.title: UK: Year 2000 may cost Mercury $133 mln - report.
newsitem.headline: Year 2000 may cost Mercury $133 mln - report.

text.p: Mercury Communications, part of Britain's second telecoms firm Cable and Wireless, could face a bill of up to 80 million pounds ($133 million) to fix a computer glitch dubbed the "millennium problem", according to a magazine.

Computer Weekly said that although Mercury Communications was only 12 years old and had implemented its information technology from scratch, it would have to dig deep into its pockets so that computers could deal with the Year 2000.

"We've budgeted for 35-40 million pounds, which the board has agreed, but it could reach 80 million pounds," the report quoted Mercury's new IT director, Uwe Natho, as saying. "But if I'm lucky, it could only by 20 million pounds," he added.

Estimates of the cost of the millennium problem to world business vary but are as high as $900 billion over the next three years -- just because most computers are programmed with a two-digit code instead of four.
This prevents them from recognising dates from the Year 2000 onwards. Information with a date beyond this could then be rejected, bringing businesses to an abrupt halt.
Natho, who is coordinating "millenium compliance" across the company, said Mercury had grabbed software wherever it could after telecoms liberalisation in Britain because it had to grow so fast.
"You name it, we've got it...In 12 years we've accumulated 422 applications," he was quoted as saying.
